rationale: B wins because it does the same four-angle architecture as A, but asks sharper kill-or-save proof questions before anyone wastes a reporter's time. A's best line, "Discord undercuts the 30% app-store toll with a 10% cut for paid communities," is strong, but B improves it with the mobile-stack test: "whether the 10% applies to subscriptions bought inside the iOS and Android apps." A is good strategist material; B is the one that has already heard the reporter's first hostile follow-up.
gaps_in_A: "a direct shot at the prevailing platform-fee structure" overstates intent. The facts support a lower fee, not Discord deliberately taking a shot.
"right before an IPO" is too hot. The update says Discord is reportedly preparing for an IPO, not that timing is imminent.
"the person who has run a large gaming community for free" invents both scale and prior monetization status. You do not have a named server, size, or evidence it was unpaid.
The fee-angle proof asks whether 10% is all-in, but misses the more precise app-store stacking question on iOS and Android. That is where the headline dies first.
gaps_in_B: "the fee comparison is Discord's own framing" is not in the supplied facts. The comparison exists in the update, but attribution to Discord is smuggled in.
"saying so out loud" decorates the fee angle with intent the update does not prove.
"if the effective mobile rate is closer to 40%" is useful as a stress test, but it is still speculative math unless the purchase path and app-store treatment are confirmed.
The trend angle still needs outside market context; "comparable take-rate and creator-earnings data" is correctly requested, but without it this is a scaffold, not yet a pitch.
